articles.title: Removing a watermark from your own MP4 without cropping the frame
articles.excerpt: If you have ever licensed footage that arrived with a distributor logo burned into the corner, you know the choice is usually bad: crop the frame and lose composition, or live with the logo. Cropping…
articles.body: If you have ever licensed footage that arrived with a distributor logo burned into the corner, you know the choice is usually bad: crop the frame and lose composition, or live with the logo. Cropping is a destructive decision. A 16:9 clip cropped to hide a corner mark is no longer 16:9 in any useful sense, and any text overlay you add later has to be repositioned around the new frame. For short social clips you can sometimes get away with it. For anything that needs the full frame, you cannot. What the problem actually is A burned-in watermark is not a layer you can toggle off. The pixels under the mark are gone; the encoder wrote the logo into the same macroblocks as the background.

articles.title: Build a Simple E-commerce MVP with AI: A Step-by-Step Guide
articles.excerpt: If you've ever typed "build me an e-commerce app" into an AI tool, you know how it goes. You get something that runs, but it's not what you pictured. The login works differently than you wanted, the c…
articles.body: If you've ever typed "build me an e-commerce app" into an AI tool, you know how it goes. You get something that runs, but it's not what you pictured. The login works differently than you wanted, the checkout has steps you never asked for, and half the buttons look like they came from different apps. The problem isn't the AI. It's that you left it hundreds of decisions to guess at. What worked for me was changing the order of things. I stopped asking for code first. Instead I ask Claude to help me write five short documents, answer its questions, and only then hand everything to Claude Code to build. The code ends up being the easy part. This post walks through the whole process with the exact prompts I use.

articles.body: TL;DR Darwin-180B-RSI , an open-weight model from Korea's VIDRAFT, scored 73.68 in mathematical and scientific reasoning on SuperCLUE's November 2026 evaluation. That is first among open-weight models and second overall, directly behind OpenAI's GPT-6.1-Sol (76.32). The largest model in the same evaluation, Moonshot AI's Kimi-K3.1-Pro at 2.8 trillion parameters, scored 63.16. Darwin has 180 billion parameters, about one sixteenth of that size, and finished more than 10 points ahead. This post explains the two techniques behind the result and what the size difference means for serving cost. The full ranking Why SuperCLUE counts as third-party verification SuperCLUE does not accept scores submitted by model developers.

articles.title: Electromechanical vs. PIN Diode RF Switches: What Actually Fails First
articles.excerpt: Every RF bench has a switch that dies young. In ATE racks and radar front ends, the switch is often the first part to fail, and it is almost never the part the designer blamed. The usual cause is a mi…
articles.body: Every RF bench has a switch that dies young. In ATE racks and radar front ends, the switch is often the first part to fail, and it is almost never the part the designer blamed. The usual cause is a mismatch between the technology chosen and the way the switch is actually driven: hot switching, DC on the RF line, or a control interface that promises more than the contact can deliver. This is not a datasheet comparison. It is the short list of things that decide which of the two switch families you should specify, and what will kill either one early. Two technologies, one decision An electromechanical (EM) coaxial switch moves a metal contact.

articles.title: This supernova impostor baffled astronomers for 15 years — until they found a hidden black hole feeding on an unstable star
articles.excerpt: A hidden black hole or neutron star companion to an unstable massive star is causing the system to erupt in light that mimics a supernova explosion.
articles.body: A cosmic imposter that has faked being a supernova 27 times and counting is actually a hot, luminous, and decidedly unstable star that is being fed on by a vampiric black hole or neutron star, NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory has discovered. When a massive star reaches the end of the road and runs out of nuclear fuel to power fusion reactions in its core, the star is destroyed in a supernova explosion. That’s what astronomers thought they had found on 11 January 2012, when they observed what appeared to be a supernova on the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, which is about 25 million light-years away in the constellation Coma Berenices. Yet when the light of the 'supernova' faded, the star was still there, only to continue bursting into light every 113 days.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 12, 2014: European Philae probe lands on Comet 67P, bounced twice and then got lost for nearly 2 years
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P, then bounced twice and got lost. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 12, 2014, a European spacecraft named Philae landed on Comet 67P . To say it was a bumpy landing would be an understatement. The European Space Agency's Philae lander separated from an orbiter called Rosetta ahead of its historic landing in 2014. It was supposed to use harpoons to secure itself on to the surface of Comet 67P, but the harpoons never fired. When it touched down, it immediately bounced back up into space . The first bounce brought Philae half a mile above the comet's surface before gravity brought it back down. Philae was missing for almost two years before scientists found it . Images from Rosetta showed Philae stuck in a dark crevice on top of the rubber duck-shaped comet.
